directions: Claret produces domed pincushion flowerheads in a deep wine-maroon shade, one of the darkest colors available in the genus, held above mounded lobed foliage on wiry branching stems. Set divisions in early spring or fall into humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist, since the plant sulks and flowers poorly if it dries out during summer heat. A site with morning sun and afternoon shade gives the richest flower color while still keeping stems sturdy and self-supporting. Cut the whole plant back hard after the first flush to encourage a second round of bloom into early autumn, and lift and divide congested clumps every three to four years.

This selection from the Somerset garden of the same name carries intensely dark crimson-red bracts surrounding a matching central boss, giving the whole flowerhead a saturated blood-red glow that darkens further as blooms age. It performs best in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in part shade, where summer heat and drought stress are moderated. Plant divisions in early spring, mulch to conserve soil moisture, and shear spent flower stems to the basal foliage after the first flowering flush to prompt repeat bloom through midsummer. Divide every three to four years in spring once the clump becomes congested or flowering declines.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

directions: Ruby Wedding is a compact, front-of-border selection with small, ruby-red pincushion flowers held over neat clumps of deeply lobed foliage, staying noticeably shorter and tidier than most Astrantia major cultivars. Grow it in evenly moist, fertile soil in partial shade, or in full sun only where summers stay cool, since drought and heat quickly cause scorched leaf margins and early dormancy. Deadhead spent flower stems regularly to extend the June-through-August bloom window and to prevent excessive self-seeding, since seedlings will not come true to the parent's compact ruby color. Lift and divide the clump every three to four years in spring to keep it vigorous and floriferous.

Shaggy (also sold as 'Margery Fish') carries unusually large, showy flowerheads: an oversized ring of long, narrow, white bracts tipped and veined in green surrounds the central pincushion, giving each bloom a distinctly ragged, spidery outline compared to the tidier cultivars of the species. Plant divisions in early spring in humus-rich soil that holds moisture well, siting the clump in partial shade to protect the papery bracts from bleaching in strong sun. Keep soil consistently moist through summer, since dry spells shorten the bloom season and can trigger early leaf dieback. Cut back after the main flush in midsummer to tidy the foliage and encourage a lighter repeat bloom in early fall, and divide congested clumps every three to four years.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

directions: Native to Siberia and the Russian Far East, this meadowsweet forms clumps of large, deeply palmate leaves topped in early to midsummer by flat, feathery plumes of pink buds opening to creamy white-pink flowers. It thrives in consistently moist to boggy soil along pond edges, streambanks, or rain gardens, and will not tolerate drying out even briefly once established. Plant divisions in spring in partial shade, where the foliage stays lush and green through summer without scorching; full sun is tolerable only where soil moisture never lapses. Mulch to retain moisture and divide the spreading clumps every three to four years in early spring to control size and renew vigor.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

directions: The largest species in the genus, Kamchatka meadowsweet sends up towering stems topped with huge, frothy plumes of fragrant creamy-white flowers well above bold, broad-lobed foliage, making a dramatic architectural statement at the back of a moist border or pond margin. Give it rich, consistently damp to wet soil and part shade, siting it where its imposing height and spread will not overwhelm smaller neighbors. It resents drying out, so mulch heavily and water deeply during dry spells, especially in its first two seasons while the root system establishes. Divide the coarse clumps in early spring only when necessary, since it resents disturbance and is slow to re-establish after division.

This double-flowered form of common meadowsweet produces denser, fluffier creamy-white flower clusters than the wild species, and stays noticeably more compact, making it easier to place in a smaller moist border or cottage-style planting. Like the species, it wants constantly moist to wet, humus-rich soil and resents summer drought, which quickly causes crisped leaf edges and early collapse. Plant divisions in spring in part shade, where the aromatic foliage stays fresher through the heat of summer than it would in full sun. Deadhead as flowers fade to tidy the planting, since this sterile double form sets little to no seed and relies on division for propagation; split congested clumps every three to four years in early spring.

common_name: Lilac Squirrel Burnet (Pendulous Fuzzy Pink-Lilac Burnet)
directions: Named for its fuzzy, drooping, bottlebrush-like flower spikes in a soft pink-lilac shade that dangle and bob like squirrel tails above blue-green pinnate foliage, this Japanese species selection blooms later in the season, from late summer into fall, than most border burnets. Plant divisions in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, choosing a site with full sun in cooler climates or light afternoon shade where summers run hot, since the foliage can scorch in prolonged heat and dry soil. Stake or grow among sturdier neighbors if the site is windy, as the arching flower stems are somewhat lax. Divide the clump every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and flower production.
